body:
We used to directly insert the value (without quotes, because it's Numeric):

```
SELECT .. WHERE id::integer = 9999999999;
```

When parsed, PostgreSQL would recognise that the right-hand literal is clearly a numeric (because it doesn't fit in anything else), and therefore we're using `numeric = numeric`. So, we'd get a slow upcast + seqscan, but it would work.

---

Now, we use a bind param:

```
SELECT .. WHERE id::integer = $1;
```

When that one is parsed, $1's type must be resolved from "unknown" to a real type. And as it's being compared with an integer, it thus follows that $1 must also be an integer.

Later, we attempt to execute our prepared statement, passing 9999999999. That won't fit in an integer -> error.

---

Incidentally, the same unknown -> integer -> error pattern can be seen if we run the query with a quoted literal:

```
SELECT .. WHERE id::integer = '9999999999';
```

---

There's no way we can avoid the immediate type-resolution of the bind parameter: that's part of what the prepare is all about.

We could force the first interpretation, by explicitly casting one side of the equality to numeric:

```
SELECT .. WHERE id::integer = $1::numeric;
```

... but that would mean a slow indexless plan for all queried values. (Or at least, the need to explicitly create a different, less efficient, index -- which is essentially equivalent.)

Thus, I believe our only option is to pre-emptively refuse to stuff an over-sized value into a bind param.

For the cases we care about, we should always have the column info. So, if we start tracking the width of integer columns (which we currently ignore), then we should have all we need to be able to refuse to DB-cast an out-of-range value.

That still leaves you raising an exception, but a far more manageable one than the inscrutable PGError we see right now.

What is the behavior of PG when we do upcast? It returns no values, right? Although raising is almost certainly the correct behavior for values outside of interest overflow range, I'm not happy with the glaring inconsistency that leaves us with. Our policy is to cast invalid input to `nil` (which of course we cannot do here)

@sgrif this actually reminded me of https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/11957 and friends :) Would it make sense to have both cases work similarly? (raising a `ENOHOPE` exception of some sort at the connection/adapter level and catch it upstream in the finders and re-raise a RecordNotFound (perhaps with its `#cause` set to the `ENOHOPE` error in case people need to differentiate it for some reason)?

An obvious place where this would break this is that going to a URL like http://myapp.com/posts/9999999999999999999999999999999 would now 500 instead of 404 (this has been true since 4.1).

Another example I ran into is [this line](https://github.com/discourse/discourse/blob/master/app/models/topic_link.rb#L132) in discourse, which caused [this test](https://github.com/discourse/discourse/blob/master/spec/models/topic_link_spec.rb#L59) to break.

When someone posts a link in a topic (or a reply, etc), it scans the content for links and try to add an inline preview snippet (see https://meta.discourse.org/t/what-is-a-onebox/4546). As a special case, if the link "looks like" an internal URL from the same site/forum, it'll try to look up that topic internally to generate that snippet rather than actually hitting the URL.

In practical terms though, is returning a 500 actually that much worse? 404 seems incorrect as well. 406 would make more sense, since we aren't looking for an ID that doesn't exist, it's a completely invalid ID that can never exist.

(I ended up "fixing" it by [changing the test](https://github.com/chancancode/discourse/commit/cc4f021af6b4ea3d99d45b7f036db27ac08a1e22), since it is supposed to test the "wrong topic ID" case, not the "super strange topic ID" case. But I believe the end result is if you try to include a link with a crazy ID in there, your post would not save and you'll get a 500)

@sgrif for the 404/500 case, I'm not sure if it's "that bad", but I'm not sure if that's something we should be "leaking". But the bigger problem is that you would not be able to do something like this "safely" anymore:

``` ruby
# Or perhaps you are in a after_save callback
Topic.transaction do
  topic = Topic.find_by(id: ...) # or just `find`

  if topic
    # Do something
  else
    # Do something else
  end
end
```

I you try to rescue the exception in the `find_by` call, you will end up with a broken transaction on PG. The only way to do this without it blowing up is to manually check if the param you are passing to the query is within the bounds of a PG integer (or whatever it happens to be), which would be pretty crazy thing to do in app code.

OK. I think the answer then is to treat this the same way we'd end up
treating a non-numeric string. I'll take a crack at this tonight.
